title: Future You Wants You To Do Two Things
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Prompted by a lottery billboard reading Future You wants you to play, Stuart asks what Future You actually wants educators to do today. His first answer is to work toward Seligman's PERMA conditions of well-being: positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning and accomplishment. His second is to harness the compound effect, illustrated by the penny that doubles daily and Darren Hardy's story of three friends whose tiny daily habits diverge dramatically after two years. He closes with Jim Burke and Doug Fisher as examples of people whose output comes from small daily commitments to reading and writing. The essay argues that a flourishing teaching life is built from penny-sized daily investments rather than dramatic overhauls.
points: Seligman's PERMA framework gives educators a checklist for the conditions of a good life, including meaning drawn from the larger public-education project.
Compounding applies to habits, with results that look flat for roughly two years before changing rapidly.
Small daily choices, such as fifteen minutes of reading or an hour of TV, diverge into very different outcomes in health, marriage and career.
Prolific professionals like Burke and Fisher attribute their output to daily reading and writing rather than talent.
The lottery ticket is a foil: consistent small investments, not a gamble, are what Future You wants.
quotes: The good things in our lives today tend to be the fruits of work that someone — us, or an inventor, or a former teacher, or our grandmothers — did some time before today. Future You does want you to do some stuff today, this week, this year.

Too many educators today feel that their work has been reduced to meaningless things like test scores or evaluation ratings; resisting such soul-sucking reductionism is something I've written a whole ebook about, but it's also as simple as keeping our eyes on a self-defined Everest as we go about our work.

If I offer you either $3 million today or a single penny that doubles in value every day for 31 days, you end up with nearly $11 million if you take the penny — more than triple the offer of $3 million cash.
Ben's not going for any kind of All or Nothing, drastic life change — he just wants to be consistent with a few small things that he knows he could easily fall into abandoning.

I once asked Jim Burke how he's managed to produce so much great work. He didn't cite his intelligence or his work ethic or any of his many giftings; rather, he said that instead of watching an hour of TV each night, he spends an hour reading or writing.
So no, New York Lottery — Future Me doesn't want me to buy a lotto ticket; Future Me wants me to make penny-sized, daily investments toward PERMA until I reap the benefits of compounding.
